transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-21 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sophie M., Liam C., Ana G. - Redwood; Priya N., Marcus L., Tess R., Ravi P. - Verdant

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): discuss POC scope for integrating Redwood inference; priorities are tool-calling for instruments, structured JSON outputs for LIMS ingestion, and meeting latency/throughput targets for daily run volumes. Benchmarks: p95 latency, token cost, and throughput under continuous batching.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie M: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about an hour. I'll kick off quick, introduce the team. Liam and Ana from our SE org will cover the SDKs and the benchmark plan.
[00:12] Priya N: Thanks. Quick context - Verdant runs a lab assistant that does protocol summaries, instrument sequencing commands, and structured output that goes directly into our LIMS. We need deterministic JSON schema responses for downstream automation.
[00:25] Marcus L: And from infra side we need to understand networking: do we go Redwood-hosted or dedicated in our VPC, what are tradeoffs. Also timeline - Q3 pilot is what we want.
[00:37] Liam C: Great. Real quick, two integration paths: 1) OpenAI-compatible REST endpoints using Redwood's hosted inference (fastest to start), or 2) Private Dedicated / VPC deployment for strict data controls. Both support SDKs (Python/Node) and function/tool calling.
[00:50] Tess R: Can the function calling reach our instrument control API? That API sits behind a private subnet.
[01:02] Ana G: Yes but with different setups. Hosted mode: function call payloads are returned in the response; Verdant would run a connector app that takes the function output and calls the instrument API from inside the customer network. For Private/VPC, we can run the connector inside the same VPC or use a secure connector service.
[01:20] Ravi P: Important: we need strongly validated JSON that matches our schema. If the model returns malformed JSON intermittently it breaks the LIMS. How do you guarantee structure?
[01:33] Liam C: We recommend combined strategies: constrained prompts with JSON schema examples, Redwood's structured-output flags and a lightweight post-processor that validates and retries using the same prompt with a 'fix' instruction. We also support dedicated constrained decoders and function signatures. Not perfect but error rates drop from ~6% to <0.5% in our internal tests for well-specified prompts.
[02:00] Priya N: Can you share examples?
[02:05] Ana G: Yes, we'll drop a repo link. Example snippet: prompt -> function call signature -> model returns a function payload with fields instrument_id, sequence_steps (array), estimated_runtime_min. Then the connector confirms and posts to LIMS. We'll share the README with schema examples.
[02:27] Marcus L: Ok. On performance - our baseline load is about 1200 protocol generation requests per day, with spikes up to 600 concurrent in a ~10 minute upload window during batch runs. Typical prompt sizes are 400-1,200 tokens. What's realistic for p95 latency?
[02:47] Liam C: For hosted Redwood endpoints using a medium-sized model variant we see p50 ~120-200ms per inference when short (under 512 tokens) with streaming off. For your 1k token prompts streaming might be needed; p95 will depend on model and batching. If you accept model variants and batching, you can target p95 ~1.2-1.6s for 1k tokens on hosted with continuous batching. If strict <300ms p95 is required for 1k tokens, we'd recommend Dedicated with tuned kernels or more powerful variants.
[03:20] Tess R: Cost is also a constraint. Do you have rough per-token numbers for the pilot?
[03:26] Sophie M: We'll put formal pricing in the SOW, but rough hosted pilot estimates are between $0.0006-$0.0012 per token depending on model family and throughput. Part of the Optimize phase is selecting quantized variants to reduce cost.
[03:40] Priya N: For acceptance criteria we want: 1) Structured output accuracy >99% for schema conformance on a 500-sample test set, 2) p95 latency under 2s for 1k-token prompts during target throughput, 3) end-to-end failure rate <0.5% over a 48-hour soak test.
[04:00] Liam C: That's reasonable and aligns with our typical pilot gates. We'll include regression tests in the benchmark harness and run canary load tests to validate.
[04:12] Marcus L: Benchmarks - what's the test harness look like? Can we run it from our infra so we measure real network hops?
[04:20] Ana G: Yes we can do a hybrid: Redwood runs a controlled micro-benchmark suite against hosted endpoints from multiple regions; Verdant can also run the same harness from your environment hitting the sandbox endpoint so you measure your network path, IP allowlist, and connector performance. We'll provide a dockerized harness that replays prompt sets at configurable QPS, records latencies, token counts, and returns CSVs and a summary dashboard.
[04:46] Ravi P: Will the harness test function calling latencies end-to-end including our connector?
[04:52] Liam C: We can. The harness supports an instrument mock receiver that can be swapped for your connector endpoint. That lets you measure round-trip time from request to instrument-ack.
[05:02] Priya N: Security - SOC2 ok, but we also need KMS integration and audit logs for every token request. How detailed are your logs and can we integrate with our SIEM?
[05:14] Sophie M: We capture request/response metadata, routing decisions, latencies and error codes. For Private deployments you can bring your own KMS/HSM and we can stream audit logs to your S3 or SIEM. For hosted we provide log exports and long-term retention as an add-on. We'll attach our SOC2 summary and a KMS integration note.
[05:33] Marcus L: Data residency - some samples must not leave EU. Is that handled?
[05:38] Ana G: Yes, we have region pinning. For mixed workloads we can route sensitive data to EU-only clusters or Dedicated capacity in your region. We'll note support for EU region availability in the SOW.
[05:50] Priya N: Ok timeline - we want pilot start in early August, full 6-week pilot. What's the ramp plan?
[05:57] Sophie M: Proposed: Week 0 (preparation) - exchange artifacts, get sandbox keys and sample dataset; Week 1 - initial integration and smoke tests; Week 2-3 - run benchmark harness and tune prompts/quantization; Week 4 - soak test and LIMS integration; Week 5-6 - validation and acceptance. We'll also schedule weekly syncs.
[06:18] Tess R: Who will do the on-prem connector work? Our side or Redwood?
[06:22] Sophie M: Usually the connector is customer-owned; Redwood will provide example connectors and help troubleshoot. For Dedicated deals we can offer services for connector dev as an add-on. We'll capture desired support level in the SOW.
[06:34] Ravi P: A concern: deterministic behavior when repeating requests. We need stable outputs for audit. Can you pin seeds or reduce sampling randomness?
[06:42] Liam C: Yes, you can use deterministic decode settings (temperature 0, top_p fixed) and pin model versions. For even more determinism we recommend using a cached prefix approach: static system prompt plus explicit function signatures. That gives very repeatable outputs for structured tasks.
[06:58] Priya N: For model variants, will there be fallbacks? If the primary model is busy, do you have graceful degrade to a cheaper/quantized variant?
[07:06] Ana G: Yes we support routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, and fallback chains. The platform can fallback to a compatible quantized variant. We'll show a config example in the SOW.
[07:18] Marcus L: Are there limits on concurrent function calls? For our spikes we might have 600 concurrent calls.
[07:25] Liam C: In hosted we handle concurrency through autoscaling but there are soft quotas; for predictable high concurrency we recommend Dedicated reserved capacity where you specify GPU pools sized for peak QPS. In the pilot we can provision burst capacity.
[07:40] Priya N: How will we validate structured output accuracy? We want a clean test harness that runs the sample set and reports schema conformance and semantic checks (e.g., step ordering).
[07:51] Ana G: We'll include schema conformance validators in the harness (JSON schema check) and you can add domain-specific validators. We'll produce per-sample logs and aggregate metrics.
[08:03] Sophie M: Quick logistics - we'll send the SOW and pilot plan by Thursday. Also sending a short checklist of what Verdant should provide (sample prompts, datasets, network constraints, acceptance criteria).
[08:12] Priya N: One more: latency targets during batch-window are harder. We'll share the exact window and concurrency curve.
[08:19] Sophie M: Great, include that in the dataset and we'll mirror it in the harness.
[08:24] Marcus L: Any regulatory paperwork for us being in healthcare-adjacent?
[08:28] Sophie M: We have a compliance packet; we'll flag relevant pages for research labs and data handling.
[08:34] Tess R: Last question - tool calling reliability. If an instrument expects a 200 OK after a command but the connector gets a duplicate or delayed message, do you have idempotency helpers?
[08:45] Liam C: We recommend connector-level idempotency keys and Redwood's function call returns include unique request IDs and timestamps. The harness can simulate duplicate deliveries.
[08:56] Priya N: Perfect. If you can include a concrete example of a full roundtrip in the README that'd help.
[09:02] Ana G: We'll add a step-by-step example: prompt -> function call -> connector -> instrument mock -> ack -> final LIMS record.
[09:10] Sophie M: Ok, I'll recap next steps: SOW + benchmark plan by Thu, sandbox credentials by Wed, Verdant provides prompts/dataset by Fri. Then kickoff next Monday. Anything else?
[09:23] Marcus L: No, that's it. Thanks.
[09:26] Priya N: Thanks all.
[09:28] [call ends]
